title: BGP Route Reflection: An Alternative to Full Mesh Internal BGP (IBGP)
summary: Describes route reflection, a method that removes the need for a full mesh of internal BGP (IBGP) sessions inside an autonomous system. A full mesh creates a serious scaling problem as the network grows. This document replaces RFC 2796 and RFC 1966. It is a draft standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Route reflection lets selected BGP routers pass routes to other internal peers. This avoids requiring every router in an autonomous system to have a direct session with every other router.

questions: what is a bgp route reflector
how does route reflection avoid loops
subtitle: How route reflectors reduce the number of internal BGP sessions an autonomous system needs.

tldr.problem: A full mesh of internal BGP speakers requires n*(n-1)/2 unique sessions, which becomes difficult to scale as the network grows.
tldr.mechanism: A route reflector can advertise selected internal BGP routes to client peers. ORIGINATOR_ID and CLUSTER_LIST attributes help routers detect reflection loops.
tldr.outcome: RFC 4456 replaces RFC 1966 and RFC 2796. The unit metadata lists RFC 7606 as an update.

today: RFC 4456 is listed in the unit metadata as a Draft Standard. It obsoletes RFC 2796 and RFC 1966, and has been updated by RFC 7606.

sections.title: The Full-Mesh Scaling Problem
sections.content:
In the usual internal BGP (IBGP) model, all BGP speakers in one autonomous system must be fully meshed. Each router needs a session with every other router, for a total of n*(n-1)/2 unique sessions when there are n speakers.

RFC 4456 describes route reflection as an alternative. A route reflector can advertise a route learned through IBGP to selected internal peers, changing the usual rule that an IBGP speaker does not re-advertise an IBGP-learned route to another IBGP speaker.
sections.plainLanguage: In a full mesh, every router needs a separate session with every other router. Route reflection lets selected routers relay routes so the full set of direct sessions is not needed.

sections.title: Design Goals
sections.content:
The design aims to be simple to configure and understand. It should allow a network to move from a full mesh without changing its topology or autonomous system.

It is also designed to allow IBGP peers that do not implement route reflection to remain in the same AS without losing BGP routing information. The RFC adds two optional, non-transitive BGP attributes to help prevent loops.
sections.plainLanguage: The method is intended to be understandable, support a gradual transition, and keep older IBGP peers in the network.

sections.title: Reflectors, Clients, and Clusters
sections.content:
A router that re-advertises routes learned from IBGP peers is a route reflector (RR). Its internal peers are divided into clients and non-clients. An RR and its clients form a cluster.

Client peers do not need to be fully meshed. Non-client peers do. In the basic example, a reflector can pass a route between two clients, removing the need for a direct IBGP session between those clients.
sections.plainLanguage: A route reflector passes routes between its clients. Clients can avoid direct sessions with one another, while non-client peers still form a full mesh.

sections.title: Route Reflection and Redundancy
sections.content:
An RR first selects its best path using its normal path-selection rule. If the best path came from a non-client, the RR reflects it to all clients. If it came from a client, the RR reflects it to all non-clients and the other clients.

An AS may use multiple RRs. In a simple arrangement, RRs are fully meshed as non-client peers and each client has an IBGP session with the RR in its cluster. Conventional BGP speakers can be clients or non-clients, allowing gradual migration.

A cluster commonly has one RR and uses that RR's BGP Identifier as its cluster identifier. To avoid a single point of failure, several RRs in one cluster can share a four-byte CLUSTER_ID, allowing an RR to discard routes received from another RR in its own cluster.
sections.plainLanguage: The reflector sends a best route to the peer groups that need it. A cluster can have more than one reflector if they share a cluster identifier.

sections.title: Detecting Reflection Loops
sections.content:
ORIGINATOR_ID is an optional, non-transitive attribute with type code 9 and a length of four bytes. An RR creates it when reflecting a route, and it records the BGP Identifier of the route's originator in the local AS. A router that recognizes its own identifier in this attribute SHOULD ignore the route.

CLUSTER_LIST is an optional, non-transitive attribute with type code 10. It records the cluster identifiers the route has passed through. An RR MUST prepend its local cluster identifier when reflecting a route. If the local identifier already appears in the list, the advertisement SHOULD be ignored.
sections.plainLanguage: Reflected routes carry identifiers showing where they started and which clusters handled them. A router can reject a route when those identifiers show that it has returned to a place it already visited.

sections.title: Effects on Route Selection
sections.content:
When a route has an ORIGINATOR_ID, the BGP tie-breaking process SHOULD treat that value as the BGP Identifier of the speaker that advertised the route. A new tie-breaking step SHOULD prefer a route with the shorter CLUSTER_LIST; a route without that attribute has length zero.

When reflecting a route, an RR SHOULD NOT change NEXT_HOP, AS_PATH, LOCAL_PREF, or MED. Configuration must not modify the loop-prevention attributes, because those changes could create routing loops.
sections.plainLanguage: If routes are otherwise tied, the route that crossed fewer clusters is preferred. Reflectors should also preserve key path attributes so their changes do not create loops.

sections.title: Configuration and Operational Limits
sections.content:
BGP does not let a client identify itself dynamically as a reflector client, so the RFC describes manual configuration. An RR reflects only its best path, which is part of how route reflection reduces the information exchanged.

Depending on the topology, MED comparisons or different IGP metrics can make route selection differ from a full IBGP mesh. The RFC discusses ways to reduce those differences, including keeping intra-cluster IGP metrics better than inter-cluster metrics and using policy to influence route selection. It recommends designing the reflection topology to match the network topology when several paths exist.

The security considerations say this extension does not change the security issues already present in IBGP.
sections.plainLanguage: Operators configure which peers are clients and plan reflectors around the network's routes. Route reflection changes how routes are shared, but does not add a new security mechanism.
